Convergence, Boundaries, and Singularity

Source: vignettes/convergence.Rmd
convergence.Rmd
library(mixeff)

fit_status() reports the convergence status of a model fitted by lmm() or glmm(). This vignette explains interior and reduced-rank solutions, the test for singularity, and the use of verify_convergence() to check a fitted optimum. It also describes what happens when the engine substitutes a different GLMM estimator.

Interior solutions

The first example is a small longitudinal study with twelve clinics, a week effect, and a treatment contrast.

fit <- lmm(
  score ~ week + treatment + (1 | clinic),
  clinic_visits,
  control = mm_control(verbose = -1)
)
fit_status(fit)
#> [1] "converged_interior"

converged_interior means the engine accepted a finite interior solution under its convergence rules, with every variance component away from zero. Individual derivative checks can still be unavailable; the certificate below records which checks completed. The status does not establish global optimality, correct model specification, or that the data carry enough information.

Three statuses distinguish the main outcomes:

  • converged_interior — the engine accepted a finite interior solution under its convergence rules.
  • converged_reduced_rank — the engine accepted a solution whose random-effect covariance has lower rank than requested.
  • not_optimized — the run stopped without certifying a stationary point, for example in a flat or boundary region. Estimates are present, but convergence has not been established. summary() also records this status in a Notes: line.

Optimization is silent and runs within one native call under bounded evaluation budgets; the lmm()/glmm() help pages and ?mm_control document the budgets and how to cap them.

optimizer_certificate() reports the optimizer, stopping condition, and checks used to assign the convergence status:

optimizer_certificate(fit)
#> Optimizer certificate:
#>                    metric                value
#>                    status   converged_interior
#>                 optimizer       pattern_search
#>                 objective     95.0585066127678
#>                iterations                   23
#>        free_gradient_norm 0.000357840060177139
#>   projected_gradient_norm 0.000357840060177139
#>         hessian_eigen_min     20.7651381551018
#>              hessian_rank                    1
#>          information_rank                    1
#>         optimizer_hessian          approximate
#>  derivative_certification          approximate
#>   optimizer_hessian: active-subspace Hessian from finite differences of the
#>     analytic gradient is positive semidefinite
#>   derivative_certification: analytic-gradient KKT check and
#>     finite-difference-of-gradient Hessian check passed

For joint-Laplace GLMMs, optimizer evidence and inference covariance are separate records. The fit-time optimizer certificate does not include a full Hessian assessment over fixed effects (beta) and covariance parameters (theta); it labels that check not_assessed, with the stage in the reason. Optimization may still compute a Hessian for polishing. The label does not mean that a Hessian computation failed.

The later inference stage attempts a central finite-difference Hessian of minus twice the log likelihood over beta and interior theta coordinates. It omits theta coordinates too close to their lower bounds for central differences. When this Hessian passes its checks, fixed-effect covariance is twice the beta block of its inverse. If that route fails, an available RX fallback conditions on theta and carries a different method and lower reliability. Inspect attr(vcov(gfit), "mm_method"), "mm_status", "mm_reliability", and "mm_notes" for the actual route and its scope. A successful inference calculation does not rewrite the fit-time certificate.

Raw gradient norms depend on parameter coordinates and are not measures of coefficient precision. Curvature-scaled stationarity evidence, when available, is recorded separately in optimizer_certificate(gfit)$raw$stationarity_decrement. Read both with their stated tolerances; a small scaled quantity does not change the qualification recorded in an approximate raw-gradient certificate.

Boundary and reduced-rank fits

The next example produces a singular fit. We simulate ten daily reaction-time measurements for each of eighteen subjects, with nearly perfectly correlated subject intercepts and slopes.

lme4::lmer() reports boundary (singular) fit for this model:

m <- suppressMessages(lme4::lmer(
  rt ~ days + (1 + days | subj),
  data = sleep_like
))
m
#> Linear mixed model fit by REML ['lmerMod']
#> Formula: rt ~ days + (1 + days | subj)
#>    Data: sleep_like
#> REML criterion at convergence: 1647.697
#> Random effects:
#>  Groups   Name        Std.Dev. Corr 
#>  subj     (Intercept) 23.682        
#>           days         3.221   1.00 
#>  Residual             20.065        
#> Number of obs: 180, groups:  subj, 18
#> Fixed Effects:
#> (Intercept)         days  
#>     239.879        9.251  
#> optimizer (nloptwrap) convergence code: 0 (OK) ; 0 optimizer warnings; 1 lme4 warnings
lme4::isSingular(m)
#> [1] TRUE

In mixeff, fit_status() reports the convergence outcome and is_singular() tests for singularity. For more detail, diagnostics() returns codes with severity and stage, while changes() compares the requested model with the effective specification and fitted result.

sfit <- lmm(
  rt ~ days + (1 + days | subj),
  sleep_like,
  control = mm_control(verbose = -1)
)

fit_status(sfit)
#> [1] "converged_reduced_rank"
is_singular(sfit)
#> [1] TRUE
diagnostics(sfit)$table[, c("code", "severity", "stage", "message")]
#>                 code severity         stage
#> 1 optimizer_recovery     info certification
#> 2 covariance_reduced     info certification
#>                                                                            message
#> 1            optimizer recovered after covariance KKT-guided restart (2x2 block 0)
#> 2 fitted covariance for (1 + days | subj) has effective rank 1 of requested rank 2
changes(sfit)
#> Model changes:
#>   Fitted covariance for (1 + days | subj): requested rank 2, fitted rank 1 [reduced_rank].
#> Stage-by-stage records available via $table.

The requested random-effect covariance for (1 + days | subj) has two dimensions: a subject intercept and a subject slope. The fitted covariance has effective rank one. This is recorded as the covariance_reduced diagnostic and the converged_reduced_rank status, which also appears when the object is printed.

print(sfit)
#> Linear mixed model fit by REML
#> Formula: rt ~ days + (1 + days | subj)
#> Fit status: converged_reduced_rank
#> Optimizer: trust_bq; iterations: 30; objective: 1647.7
#> nobs: 180, sigma: 20.065, logLik: -823.849
#> Fixed effects:
#> (Intercept)        days 
#>   239.87900     9.25095 
#> 
#> Fitted covariance state:
#> The fitted covariance matrix is rank-deficient.
#>   r0: requested rank 2; fitted effective rank 1.
#> Use changes(fit) to see which dimension was unsupported.
#> Use random_options(spec, group = subj) to inspect lower-dimensional covariance choices.
#> Audit verbs: audit(), diagnostics(), inference_table(), model_report()

A reduced-rank covariance does not automatically invalidate the model, but it restricts the inference methods available in mixeff. These restrictions are described at the end of this vignette.

How singularity relates to θ and rank

To read the boundary structure itself, look at the model’s internal coordinates. The random-effect covariance Σ is not optimized directly. The engine searches over a vector θ that fills a lower-triangular factor Λ, with Σ = σ²ΛΛᵀ; θ is by construction exactly the set of free entries of Λ. This is the parameterization Bates et al. (2015) describe for lme4; MixedModels.jl and the engine behind mixeff inherit it. parameterization() shows the mapping for the singular fit:

parameterization(sfit)$table[, c("theta_name", "theta_value", "lambda_value")]
#>                     theta_name  theta_value lambda_value
#> 1 theta[0:intercept,intercept] 1.180242e+00 1.180242e+00
#> 2      theta[0:days,intercept] 1.605414e-01 1.605414e-01
#> 3           theta[0:days,days] 1.678443e-08 1.678443e-08

The diagonal entry for the days slope is pinned at numerical zero — that is the boundary event behind the converged_reduced_rank status.

A zero entry in θ does not always imply singularity. A zero off-diagonal entry of Λ can occur in a full-rank covariance. In the two-dimensional example below, it sets the covariance to zero. In larger blocks, covariance entries are sums of products, so one zero factor entry need not make the corresponding covariance zero.

Singularity depends on the rank of the whole covariance matrix. For this square triangular factor, it occurs exactly when at least one diagonal entry of Λ is zero. The following example contrasts the two cases:

l11 <- 1.2
l21 <- 0.4
l22 <- 0.9

# Zero the OFF-DIAGONAL entry (l21 = 0): zero covariance, full rank.
L_offdiag_zero <- matrix(c(l11, 0, 0, l22), nrow = 2)
Sigma_offdiag_zero <- L_offdiag_zero %*% t(L_offdiag_zero)
Sigma_offdiag_zero
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,] 1.44 0.00
#> [2,] 0.00 0.81
eigen(Sigma_offdiag_zero, symmetric = TRUE)$values
#> [1] 1.44 0.81

# Zero a DIAGONAL entry (l22 = 0): the rank collapses to 1.
L_diag_zero <- matrix(c(l11, l21, 0, 0), nrow = 2)
Sigma_diag_zero <- L_diag_zero %*% t(L_diag_zero)
Sigma_diag_zero
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,] 1.44 0.48
#> [2,] 0.48 0.16
eigen(Sigma_diag_zero, symmetric = TRUE)$values
#> [1] 1.600000e+00 4.241052e-17

With the off-diagonal at zero, both eigenvalues are positive: the intercept and slope are uncorrelated, and each still has its own variance — a full-rank fit with the covariance structure specified by (1 + days || subj). With a diagonal entry at zero, one eigenvalue is zero and the two random effects collapse onto a single dimension: that is singularity.

is_singular() follows lme4’s tolerance rule: it checks whether a zero-bounded diagonal θ is below tol (default 1e-4). For older fits without a theta map, it falls back to the recorded engine covariance and fit statuses. A tolerance-based result can differ from an exact rank verdict.

Verifying an optimum: verify_convergence()

A convergence status describes the run that produced the fit. To check the stability of that solution, verify_convergence() re-runs the fit under the engine’s bounded verification workflow: a restart from the fitted optimum, one or more jittered restarts, and (LMM-only, opt-in) an alternate-optimizer consensus pass. The engine judges agreement against explicit tolerances on the objective, θ, and the fixed effects, and returns the verdict for R to format.

The R bridge reuses a live fitted handle or restores the saved fitted state before invoking that workflow. Verification compares its deliberate searches against the recorded solution, including after reload. If neither a valid handle nor a compatible snapshot is available, verification refuses rather than optimizing a replacement baseline.

vc <- verify_convergence(fit)
vc
#> Convergence verification (status: restart_agrees)
#>   restart from fitted theta agrees with the recorded optimum
#> Runs:
#>                 label      optimizer return_code objective_value
#>  restart_from_optimum pattern_search     SUCCESS         95.0585
#>      jitter_restart_1 pattern_search     SUCCESS         95.0585
#>  objective_delta theta_delta beta_delta agrees
#>      0.00000e+00 0.00000e+00 0.0000e+00   TRUE
#>      1.18234e-10 3.20312e-07 3.9968e-15   TRUE
#> Tolerances: objective 1e-05; theta 0.001; beta 1e-04

The verdict summarizes agreement with the reference optimum within the printed tolerances (restart_agrees, optimizer_consensus, fragile, unstable, or not_run). A verdict of restart_agrees is evidence of a stable optimum — the bounded re-runs came back to the same place — not proof of a global one. The consensus pass defaults to FALSE because this vendored build compiles without the optional nlopt backend; for some models the engine’s alternate optimizer choice is an nlopt optimizer, and its absence would read as a spurious fragile verdict that reflects the build, not the fit.

Verification and rank are different questions. Running the verifier on the singular fit from above also comes back restart_agrees: a reduced-rank optimum can be stable across restarts.

vs <- verify_convergence(sfit)
vs$status
#> [1] "restart_agrees"

The GLMM method uses the same workflow with wider default tolerances — objective 1e-4 and beta 1e-3, against the LMM defaults of 1e-5 and 1e-4 — because GLMM objective evaluations include inner-PIRLS numerical error and the joint path’s derivative-free beta search bounds beta reproducibility at its stopping tolerance. The consensus pass is refused for GLMM fits (the GLMM fitting routines select their own optimizers).

gfit <- glmm(
  y ~ x + (1 | g),
  trial,
  family = binomial(),
  control = mm_control(verbose = -1)
)

gv <- verify_convergence(gfit)
gv
#> Convergence verification (status: restart_agrees)
#>   restart from fitted theta agrees with the recorded optimum
#> Runs:
#>                 label optimizer                return_code objective_value
#>  restart_from_optimum  trust_bq JOINT_LAPLACE:FTOL_REACHED         179.457
#>      jitter_restart_1  trust_bq JOINT_LAPLACE:FTOL_REACHED         179.457
#>  objective_delta theta_delta  beta_delta agrees
#>      2.84217e-14 3.70270e-12 1.83527e-11   TRUE
#>      5.68434e-14 4.26725e-12 2.10366e-11   TRUE
#> Tolerances: objective 1e-04; theta 0.001; beta 0.001

GLMM estimator substitution

glmm(method = "joint_laplace") requests the joint-Laplace estimator, which supports Wald inference when the fitted covariance passes its checks. On some designs, the engine cannot certify a joint-Laplace optimum and returns a fit from the profiled-PIRLS estimator instead. The substitution is recorded in several places:

  • optimizer_certificate(fit)$raw$estimator_substitution contains the requested and effective methods, the requested method’s fit status and return code, and the reason for substitution. Use this record in scripts.
  • A condition of class mm_estimator_substitution_notice reports the change when the fit returns. Suppress it with mm_control(verbose = -1).
  • summary() prints an estimator substitution: note naming both estimators, regardless of verbosity settings or the fallback fit’s convergence status.
  • verify_convergence() restores and checks the effective estimator that produced the returned estimates.

When no substitution occurred, the record is absent:

optimizer_certificate(gfit)$raw$estimator_substitution
#> NULL

For example, in a reproduction of a published glmer() analysis of OSF study data, an error-rate model included an open-practice × year interaction. With raw, uncentered Year, the joint-Laplace fit did not certify and the engine returned a profiled-PIRLS fallback with Wald inference withheld. Centering the predictor as Year - 2015 allowed the joint fit to certify and agree with glmer() on the same data. A scaling advisory identifies the poorly scaled columns; centering or rescaling them can improve optimization.

Inference at a boundary

On singular fits, mixeff withholds Satterthwaite and Kenward–Roger degrees of freedom under its validated-support policy. The results include reason codes, and parametric bootstrap tests remain available. See vignette("inference") for the methods, restrictions, and examples.

References

  • Bates, D., Mächler, M., Bolker, B., and Walker, S. (2015). Fitting linear mixed-effects models using lme4. Journal of Statistical Software, 67(1), 1–48. https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v067.i01
